messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

For most of his career, Arun Vong had been the surgeon other people trusted when a case became chaotic. At seventy-seven, he still worked part-time in a Boston hospital, moving more slowly than he once had but with the same exacting standards. The event he describes happened during an emergency operation several months before he sought help. A young man had come in after a house fire with massive injuries, and the operating room filled with the faint, sickening smell of burned material that clung even after the patient was draped. Arun remembers the abrupt cold against his hands and forearms from prep solution and the overcooled operating room, the burst of alarms and shouted requests, and the terrible sense that the team was trying to catch up to damage that had already outrun them. The patient died on the table. What Arun recalls now is not a clean sequence but fragments that refuse to stay in order: the smell, the cold on his skin, a monitor sounding, someone calling for more blood. At times there is no image at all, only a sudden wave of the same dread and helplessness he felt then. He says the memory can feel strangely detached, “as if it happened to another surgeon,” yet the emotion arrives in full force.

In the weeks that followed, those fragments began forcing themselves into ordinary moments. A whiff of something burnt from a toaster in the hospital lounge, the particular chill of scrub room air on his arms, or simply the pressure of a stressful case would set off a reaction before he had consciously placed why. His shoulders would jerk, his body tightening at a dropped instrument or a slammed door, and he became acutely alert to unexpected sounds in the OR and at home. He had come to believe that his body had become an enemy, reacting as if danger were present even when he knew, intellectually, that he was safe. That frightened him almost as much as the death itself. If his own body could betray him like this, he thought, then something in him must be fundamentally wrong. He grew convinced that a person had to stay constantly careful because disaster could erupt without warning, and this conviction kept him scanning the room, listening for sudden noise, bracing for the next shock.

Those appraisals changed how he understood his memory of the case. Because the recollection was disordered and oddly alien, Arun took that as evidence of defect rather than injury; a competent surgeon, he felt, should be able to account for what happened in proper sequence. When only raw emotion came without pictures, he interpreted that surge as proof that his body was still out of control. The more he judged himself in this way, the less ownership he felt over the memory, and the more the event seemed to break apart into disconnected sensory pieces rather than a story he could place in the past.

He responded by trying to master it privately. When stress at work or the smell of something scorched brought the case close, he would push the thoughts down immediately and refuse to let himself dwell on them. He stopped watching medical dramas, news coverage of fires, and even documentaries that might contain emergency scenes. More surprisingly to his wife, he also began pushing away moments of pleasure. If a dinner out felt warm and easy, or a grandchild’s joke made him laugh, he would abruptly go quiet, as though positive feeling itself were unsafe. He explained that letting his guard down felt reckless. When he was already jumpy from a loud sound or keyed up during a difficult procedure, suppressing the memory seemed like the only way to keep functioning.

Over time these habits narrowed his life and fed the problem he was trying to control. By cutting off reminders in media and forcing away thoughts whenever they arose, he never arrived at a settled account of the operating-room death; the memory remained fractured, heavy with feeling but thin on order, and stress could summon the emotion without warning. Pushing away good moments left him tense even at home, which made him more sensitive to small triggers: the heat clicking on and then cold air across his skin, a charred smell from cooking, the ambient strain of a busy surgical morning. Once triggered, he became more watchful and easily startled, and in that keyed-up state the fragments of the case felt closer, not farther away. At work this took a dangerous form. Arun began taking unnecessary risks in surgery—standing longer than was wise, refusing relief, pressing through fatigue with a grim determination that sounded to him like discipline but worried younger colleagues. He told himself he had to prove he was still reliable, yet the same urgency came from his conviction that one could never be too careful and from a body that seemed perpetually prepared for catastrophe.

His marriage has grown quieter around all this. His wife sees him recoil at the smell of burnt food, fall silent during tense television commercials, and start hard at noises he once ignored. He finally agreed to seek help after freezing briefly in the operating room when cold prep solution touched his wrist and an instrument clattered to the floor; for a moment he felt the old terror with no picture attached, only certainty that something awful was about to happen. What he fears most is not simply remembering the patient’s death, but discovering that he has become the kind of surgeon—and the kind of man—who can no longer trust his own mind or body. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is to feel that the event belongs in his past rather than erupting into his present.

violation_explanations: The vignette names triggers and describes avoidance/suppression, but it does not clearly state in the same paragraph that triggers themselves lead to maladaptive strategies.
